title: Fall Asleep Fast 🌙 8 Gentle Stories on a Rainy Night | Snortlo
intro:
Hello, and welcome to Snortlo. Tonight I have eight gentle stories for you, all of them set on rainy evenings, read slowly, with the soft sound of rain falling in the background.

You don't need to do anything at all. Get comfortable. Pull the blanket up a little higher, and dim the lights, if you haven't already.

And you don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off during the first story, or the second, that's perfectly fine. The stories will keep going quietly without you.

Let's take one slow breath together. In, and out.

Let's begin.

stories.title: The Lock Keeper
stories.text:
On a quiet stretch of canal, where the water ran slow and brown between two lines of willow trees, there was a little stone cottage with a red door. Next to the cottage was a lock, with two heavy wooden gates and a pair of long black beams for pushing them open. The man who lived in the cottage was called Walt, and he had been the lock keeper there for a very long time.

Walt knew the canal the way you know the creaks in your own stairs. He knew which ducks nested under the far bank, and which heron liked to stand on the third post from the bridge, perfectly still, pretending to be a branch. He knew that the water smelled different before rain, a little cooler and greener, and he knew that on evenings like this one, the boats came slowly, one at a time, and that there was no reason at all to hurry them.

The rain had started just after tea. It was the soft kind, the kind that does not fall so much as drift. It settled on the willow leaves and gathered into drops and let go, one by one, into the canal, making small round rings that spread out and touched each other and faded. Walt put on his old green coat and his wide brimmed hat, and he took his lantern from the hook by the door.

He stepped outside and stood for a moment under the little porch roof, listening. Pat, pat, pat on the hat. A gentle hush over the water. Somewhere down the towpath, a blackbird was singing its last song of the day, as if it did not mind the rain at all.

The first boat came around the bend just as the light was turning grey. It was a long narrowboat painted dark blue, with yellow flowers in pots along its roof and a thin curl of smoke rising from its little chimney. A woman stood at the back with her hand on the tiller, wrapped in a raincoat, and a small brown dog sat beside her, looking very serious about the whole thing.

Walt raised his lantern and gave a slow wave. The woman waved back. The dog did not wave, but its tail moved once, politely.

Walt walked to the end of the lock and leaned his back against the long black beam. He pushed, and the gate began to move, slowly, the way it always did, with a deep wooden groan and a gurgle of water underneath. He did not push hard. The gates were old, and they liked to be asked nicely. Step by step, the gate swung open, and the dark water inside the lock lay flat and waiting.

The narrowboat slid in, so slowly it hardly seemed to move at all. The woman stepped onto the side with a rope and looped it around a post, and the boat settled against the wall with a soft bump.

Evening, said Walt.

Evening, said the woman. Lovely weather for ducks.

It is, said Walt. They've been very pleased with themselves all afternoon.

The woman laughed, and the dog looked at Walt as if to say that it, too, had noticed the ducks, and had opinions about them.

Walt closed the gate behind the boat. Then he walked to the other end of the lock, to the top gates, where the water was higher, and he took the windlass from his coat pocket. It was an old iron handle, worn smooth by years of hands. He fitted it onto the paddle gear and began to turn it, round and round, click by click.

Down below, a little door in the gate opened, and water from the upper canal began to pour into the lock. It made a wonderful sound, a deep, rushing, rolling sound, like a bath being filled in a house far away. The water swirled around the narrowboat, and little by little, the boat began to rise.

This was the part Walt liked best. He would stand at the edge with his lantern and watch the boat come up out of the shadows, slowly, slowly, until the flowers on the roof were level with his boots, and then level with his knees, and then the whole boat was floating beside him on the bright, full water, as if the canal had lifted it up on the palm of its hand.

The rain kept falling. It made a soft pattering on the boat roof and a quieter pattering on Walt's hat. The lantern light shone on the wet stones and turned them gold.

When the water inside the lock was level with the water outside, the rushing sound faded to a whisper, and then to nothing. Walt leaned on the top gate and pushed it open, slow and easy, and the narrowboat drifted out into the upper canal.

Thank you, called the woman.

Safe travels, said Walt. There's a good mooring just past the bridge, under the big oak. Nice and sheltered.

The woman nodded, and the dog gave one more polite tail wag, and the blue boat slipped away into the misty evening, its chimney smoke drifting sideways, its little window glowing orange.

Walt closed the gate behind it and went back to the cottage porch to wait.

The second boat came almost an hour later. By then it was nearly dark, and the rain had settled into a steady, gentle rhythm. This boat was small and green and very old, and it was steered by an old man in a knitted hat who Walt had known for many years. His name was Henry, and he travelled the canal every autumn to visit his sister, who lived three villages up.

Henry, said Walt.

Walt, said Henry.

That was mostly how their conversations went, and they both liked it that way.

Walt opened the gates, and Henry's boat slid into the lock, and Walt turned the windlass, click, click, click, and the water rushed in, and the green boat rose up out of the dark. While it rose, Henry reached into his cabin and came out with a paper bag.

From my sister, he said. She made too many.

Inside the bag were four oat biscuits, still a little warm, wrapped in a napkin. Walt thanked him, and Henry nodded, and the boat floated up, level and calm, and Henry steered it out through the top gates and away.

Good night, Walt, he called over his shoulder.

Good night, Henry.

Walt stood for a while after the boat had gone, listening to the rain. The heron had left its post. The blackbird had stopped singing. The canal was dark and smooth, with only the soft rings of the raindrops moving on its surface, and the distant orange glow of Henry's window getting smaller and smaller until it was gone around the bend.

There would be no more boats tonight. Walt was sure of it. He could feel it the way you can feel that a house has gone to sleep.

He closed the gates one last time, gently, and checked the paddles, and hung the windlass back on its hook by the door. He went inside and took off his wet coat and his wet hat and hung them by the stove to dry, where they began to steam a little, very slowly, and smell of rain and wool.

He put the kettle on. While it warmed, he set two of Henry's sister's biscuits on a plate and saved the other two for the morning. He sat in his armchair by the window, with a blanket over his knees, and watched the lantern outside the door making a small golden circle on the wet path.

The kettle began to hum, and then to sing. Walt made his tea and held the warm cup in both hands. Outside, the rain kept falling on the canal, on the willow trees, on the sleeping ducks under the far bank, on the two old gates that had done their work and were resting now, quiet and still.

Walt finished his tea. He ate the last crumb of biscuit. He listened to the rain for a little longer, and then a little longer still.

Then he reached over, and turned down the lamp, and let the soft sound of the water carry him off to sleep.

stories.title: The Baker's Cat
stories.text:
Every bakery has a smell, and every smell has a time of day. The little bakery on Elm Lane smelled of flour and cold stone at midnight, of yeast and warm water at two in the morning, and by four, when the first loaves went into the oven, it smelled like the inside of a hug.

The cat who lived there knew all of these smells by heart. She was a large, soft, orange cat called Marmalade, and she had decided, a long time ago, that she was in charge of quality.

Nobody had asked her to be. Mrs. Lowe, who owned the bakery, had simply found her one rainy autumn sitting on the back step, looking at the door as if she had been expecting it to open for quite some time. Mrs. Lowe had opened it. Marmalade had walked in, inspected the flour sacks, sniffed the oven, sat down on the warmest corner of the counter, and stayed.

That had been nine years ago. In all that time, Marmalade had never missed a morning.

On this particular night, the rain had been falling since the evening. It drummed softly on the bakery's tin roof, a gentle, steady sound, like fingertips on a table. The windows were dark, and the street outside was empty and shining, with little streams running along the edge of the pavement and down into the drains with a quiet gurgle.

Mrs. Lowe arrived at half past one, as she always did, shaking the rain from her umbrella in the doorway and stamping her boots on the mat. Marmalade was waiting on the counter. She blinked slowly, which, in cat, means good morning, you are a little late, but I forgive you.

Good morning, my love, said Mrs. Lowe. Wet out there.

Marmalade agreed with a short, low sound in her throat.

Mrs. Lowe turned on the lamps, one by one. The first was the small lamp over the sink, and then the long lamp over the big wooden table, and then the warm yellow lamp by the oven. The bakery came out of the dark slowly, like a room in a dream, all soft corners and golden light.

She tied on her apron and washed her hands and lifted the cloth from the big bowl of dough she had left to rise the night before. It had grown round and smooth and pale, and it gave a tiny sigh when she touched it. Marmalade leaned forward to look. She did not touch the dough. She was a professional. But she looked at it carefully, from one side and then the other, and then she sat back down, satisfied.

Mrs. Lowe floured the table. She turned out the dough and began to fold it, push and fold, push and fold, in a slow and steady rhythm that matched the rain on the roof. Her hands knew the work so well that she did not need to think about it, and so she hummed instead, an old tune with no words that she had learned from her mother.

Marmalade's eyes grew half closed. The humming, the rain, the soft thump of the dough on the table. It was her favourite music.

When the dough was ready, Mrs. Lowe cut it into pieces and shaped each one into a loaf. Round ones for the window. Long ones for the baskets. Two little plaited ones, shiny with egg, for the old couple who came in every Saturday and always asked for the plaited ones, and always said they were the best in town.

She lined the loaves up on wooden boards and covered them with clean cloths, so they could rise one last time. Then she put the kettle on, and sat on her tall stool by the oven, and waited.

This was the quiet hour. The rain on the roof. The tick of the clock by the door. The oven slowly warming, with little clicks and ticks of its own. Mrs. Lowe drank her tea. Marmalade washed one paw, slowly and thoroughly, and then the other.

Outside, a single car went by on the wet street, its tires making a long, soft hiss. Then nothing. Just the rain.

At four o'clock, the oven was ready. Mrs. Lowe slid the loaves inside, one board at a time, and closed the heavy door. Almost at once, the smell began. First faint, then warm, then wonderful, filling the bakery and drifting out under the front door and into the rainy street, where nobody was awake to smell it except a fox going home along the gutter, who paused, and sniffed, and thought about it very seriously before moving on.

While the bread baked, Mrs. Lowe made the rolls and the buns, and set out the trays, and wrote the day's specials on the little chalkboard in her careful round letters. Cinnamon buns. Rye loaf. Soup of the day, leek and potato.

Marmalade watched all of it. Now and then she shifted on the counter to get a better view, or to find a warmer spot, or simply because a cat likes to remind the room that she is there.

At last, the timer went. Mrs. Lowe opened the oven, and a great warm breath of bread rolled out into the room. She lifted the loaves out one by one with her big wooden paddle, and set them on the cooling racks, golden and brown, crackling very softly as they met the cooler air. If you listen to fresh bread, it sings. A tiny, crackling song, like rain on dry leaves.

And now came the most important part of the whole morning.

Marmalade stood up. She stretched, front legs first and then back legs, with great dignity. She walked along the counter, slowly, to the cooling racks, and she began her inspection.

She did not touch the loaves. She never did. She simply walked past each one, and paused, and sniffed the air above it, and looked at it with her wise green eyes. Round loaf, good. Long loaf, good. Rye loaf, very good. The two little plaited loaves, she looked at the longest of all, and then she gave a short, approving sound, and moved on.

When she reached the end of the row, she turned around, walked back to her warm corner by the oven, and lay down with her paws tucked underneath her.

Mrs. Lowe smiled. Thank you, inspector, she said. All passed, then?

Marmalade closed her eyes. All passed.

Outside, the rain was easing. The sky over the rooftops had turned from black to a deep, soft blue, and somewhere a bird was trying out the first notes of the morning. Soon the street would wake up. Soon the lamps would come on in the windows, and the first customers would come in shaking their umbrellas, and the little bell over the door would ring, and ring again.

But not yet. For now there was only the bakery, warm and golden, full of bread, and the gentle sound of the last of the rain on the roof.

Mrs. Lowe sat back down on her stool with a fresh cup of tea. Beside her, Marmalade's breathing grew slow and deep, and her whiskers twitched once, as if she was dreaming of a very good loaf.

And the rain whispered on, softer, and softer, until it was almost nothing at all.

stories.title: The Tailor's Last Coat
stories.text:
Above a shoe shop on a narrow street, up a flight of creaky wooden stairs, there was a small room with a sloping ceiling and one round window. In the room there was a long table, a tall mirror, a sewing machine as old as the building, and a man called Theo, who was a tailor.

Theo did not make many new clothes anymore. Mostly he mended things. A torn pocket. A loose button. Trousers that needed to be a little longer, because a boy had grown, or a little shorter, because a grandmother had shrunk, as grandmothers sometimes do. People climbed his creaky stairs with their favourite clothes folded over their arms, and they left them with him, and a few days later the clothes were better than before.

On this rainy evening, there was only one job left on his table. It was a long winter coat, deep grey wool, with big round buttons the colour of chestnuts. It belonged to a woman called Rose, who lived at the end of the street and walked her dog past the shoe shop every morning. She had brought the coat in on Monday.

It drags in the puddles, she had said, holding up the hem, which was muddy and a little frayed. I love it, but it's too long. I keep stepping on it on the stairs.

Leave it with me, Theo had said. I'll have it ready before the cold comes.

The cold was coming. Theo could feel it in the window glass, which was cool to the touch, and he could hear it in the rain, which had grown heavier since supper and was now drumming on the sloped roof just above his head, steady and comfortable, like a clock with a soft heart.

He switched on the lamp over his table. It was an old brass lamp with a green shade, and it made a warm circle of light on the grey wool, so that everything outside the circle went dim and soft and far away. He put on his glasses. He threaded his needle. He took a long, slow breath.

Then he began.

First, he laid the coat flat on the table, smoothing it out with both hands, the way you might smooth a blanket on a bed. The wool was thick and soft and smelled faintly of cedar and of rain. He found the line he had marked on Monday with a little piece of chalk, a pale line running all the way around the bottom of the coat, just a hand's width above the old hem.

He took his big scissors from their hook. They were heavy and cool and very sharp, and they made a lovely sound when they cut, a slow, crisp sound, like someone walking on fresh snow. Snip, snip, snip, all the way around the coat, following the chalk line. The old muddy hem fell away onto the table in one long ribbon. Theo rolled it up and set it aside. You never know when a piece of good wool will come in useful.

Now came the slow part. The part Theo liked best.

He folded the new edge of the coat up, a little at a time, and pinned it. One pin, then a little gap, then another pin. Silver pins in grey wool, shining in the lamplight like tiny stars in a cloudy sky. He worked his way all around, and when he had finished, he held the coat up to the lamp and looked at it. The fold was even. The line was straight. Good.

Then he sat back down and began to sew.

He did not use the old machine for this. A hem on a good winter coat should be sewn by hand, Theo believed, with small stitches that hide inside the fold, so that nobody can see them from the outside. It takes longer. It takes much longer. But that is the point.

In and out went the needle. In and out. Each stitch tiny, each one pulled gently tight, never too tight, so the wool would not pucker. The rain drummed on the roof. The lamp hummed very quietly. Down in the street, someone went by under an umbrella, their footsteps splashing softly, and then they were gone, and there was only the rain again.

Theo's mind drifted while his hands worked. He thought about the first coat he had ever made, long ago, when he was a young apprentice in a much bigger shop with much bigger windows. It had been for his own father, and it had been far from perfect. One sleeve was a little longer than the other. But his father had worn it every winter for twenty years, and had always said it was the warmest coat he owned.

Theo smiled to himself, and pulled the thread through, and made another tiny stitch.

Halfway around the hem, he stopped for tea. He kept a small kettle on a shelf by the window, and a tin of shortbread, and a chipped blue mug that he had used for so long it felt like part of his hand. He stood by the round window while the kettle warmed, and looked out at the street below.

The street lamps were on, each one making a little pool of orange light on the wet pavement. The rain was falling straight down, in long silver threads, as if the sky were sewing the town together. Across the road, a light was on in an upstairs window, and someone was reading in an armchair. Further along, the bakery was dark. Everything was quiet, and wet, and peaceful.

The kettle clicked. Theo made his tea, and ate one piece of shortbread, and then, after a moment's thought, a second piece. Then he went back to the table, and to the coat, and picked up his needle again.

In and out. In and out.

By the time he reached the end of the hem, it was late. The rain had softened to a gentle patter. His tea had gone cold in the blue mug. He tied off the last stitch with a small knot, tucked it neatly inside the fold where no one would ever find it, and snipped the thread.

Then he took out all the pins, one by one, and put them back in their little round tin, where they settled with a tiny silver clink.

He warmed his old iron and pressed the new hem, slowly, with a damp cloth between the iron and the wool. The steam rose up in soft clouds, smelling of warm wool and clean water, and the hem lay down flat and smooth and crisp, as if it had always been that way.

Theo hung the coat on the tall mirror stand and stepped back to look at it. It was perfect. Long enough to keep out the wind, short enough to stay out of the puddles. Not a single stitch showed.

He found a sheet of brown paper and wrote a note in his slow, careful handwriting. For Rose. Ready for the cold. Mind the stairs. He pinned the note to the collar.

Then he switched off the old machine, and tidied his scissors back onto their hook, and swept the threads from the table into his hand. He turned off the brass lamp last of all.

The room went soft and dark. The round window glowed faintly with the light of the street. The rain kept tapping on the roof, gently, steadily, like a very small tailor, sewing the night closed.

And Theo put on his own old coat, the comfortable brown one he had made for himself many winters ago, and went down the creaky stairs, and home to bed.

stories.title: Bringing the Cows Home
stories.text:
At the bottom of a long green valley, where a little river wound between the fields like a ribbon someone had dropped, there was a farm with a white house and a red barn and eleven brown cows. The farmer's name was Nora. She had a wide hat, a long waxed coat, and a voice that the cows had known since they were calves.

Every evening, just before dusk, Nora walked up the lane to the top field to bring the cows home. She had done it every evening for so many years that she no longer needed to look at the clock. She could tell the time by the light, and by the birds, and by the cows themselves, who would begin, around the same hour every day, to drift slowly toward the gate, as if they had suddenly remembered something important waiting for them in the barn.

On this evening, a light rain was falling. Not a storm. Just a fine, soft rain, so gentle that you could hardly see it falling, only feel it on your face, cool and fresh, like the mist from a waterfall far away. It made the grass shine. It made the stone walls dark. It made the whole valley smell of earth and wet leaves and something green and sweet that has no name.

Nora pulled on her boots by the back door. Her old sheepdog, a grey and white dog called Pip, was already waiting on the step, his tail sweeping slowly back and forth over the wet stone.

Ready, Pip? said Nora.

Pip was always ready. That was one of the best things about Pip.

They set off up the lane together. The lane was narrow and stony, with high hedges on both sides, and the hedges were full of small sounds. A wren rustling. A blackbird scolding. The tiny tick, tick of raindrops falling from one leaf to the next. Nora walked slowly, with her hands in her coat pockets, and Pip trotted ahead, stopping now and then to sniff something interesting at the bottom of the hedge, and then hurrying to catch up.

At the top of the lane there was a wooden gate, grey with age and soft with moss. Beyond it lay the top field, wide and sloping, with a single old oak tree standing in the middle like a great green umbrella. And under the oak tree, sheltering from the rain, were the cows.

They were all there. Nora counted them anyway, as she always did. One, two, three, all the way to eleven. Daisy, the oldest, who was always at the front. Bramble and Clover, who were sisters and never more than a few steps apart. Little Hazel, the youngest, who was still curious about everything and would sometimes stop in the middle of the field to stare at a butterfly for a very long time.

Nora leaned on the gate and called to them. It was not a shout. It was a long, low, rolling call, the same one she used every evening, a sound that rose and fell like a song with no words.

Come on, girls. Come on home.

Under the oak tree, eleven heads lifted. Eleven pairs of ears turned toward the gate. And then, slowly, without any fuss at all, Daisy began to walk.

She walked the way old cows walk, steady and unhurried, placing each foot carefully on the wet grass. Behind her came Bramble and Clover, side by side. Then the others, one by one, falling into a long, loose line that wound across the field toward the gate. Little Hazel came last, stopping to sniff a clump of clover, then remembering, and trotting to catch up with a small surprised moo.

Pip sat beside the gate and watched them come. He did not need to do anything. He knew these cows, and they knew him. His job, on evenings like this, was mostly to sit very still and look important, which he did beautifully.

Nora opened the gate wide and stepped back. Daisy walked through first, and gave Nora a long, warm look as she passed, and a soft breath through her nose that smelled of grass. Nora patted her neck. Good girl, Daisy.

One by one, the cows came through the gate and into the lane. Their hooves made a gentle, hollow sound on the stones. Clop, clop. Clop, clop. Their breath made little clouds in the cool, damp air. The rain settled on their brown backs in tiny silver beads, and they did not mind it at all.

Nora closed the gate behind Hazel and followed them down the lane. This was her favourite part of every day. The slow walk home, behind the cows, with the hedges on either side and the rain falling softly and the light fading from gold to grey to a deep, gentle blue. Nobody hurried. There was no reason to hurry. The barn would still be there. Supper would still be there. The evening would wait for them.

Halfway down the lane, the cows stopped, all at once, the way cows sometimes do, for no reason that anyone has ever understood. Nora stopped too. She stood in the lane and waited, and listened to the rain on her hat, and the river murmuring somewhere below, and a wood pigeon calling from the trees on the far side of the valley. Coo, coo, coo. Coo, coo.

After a while, Daisy decided it was time to go on, and so they all went on.

At the bottom of the lane, the barn doors stood open, and a lamp was already glowing inside, warm and yellow against the blue evening. Nora had lit it before she left. The cows walked in without being asked, each one going to her own place along the wall, where there was fresh straw and sweet hay waiting. The barn smelled of hay and warm animals and old wood, and the rain made a soft drumming on its roof that was the most comfortable sound in the world.

Nora walked along the row, giving each cow a pat and a word. Good girl, Bramble. Good girl, Clover. Good girl, Hazel, you little dreamer. She checked their water. She shook out a little more hay where it was needed. Pip lay down in the straw by the door, rested his chin on his paws, and let out a long, contented sigh.

When everything was done, Nora stood in the doorway for a moment and looked back at them. Eleven brown cows, dry and warm and munching quietly in the lamplight. The steady sound of chewing. A soft shuffle of hooves in the straw. The rain on the roof. Outside, the valley had gone dark, and the first lights were coming on in the farmhouses far away, small and gold, like stars that had come down to rest.

Good night, girls, said Nora.

She turned down the lamp until it was only a small glow. She slid the barn door almost closed, leaving a little gap for the air. Then she and Pip walked across the yard to the white house, where the kitchen window was bright and the kettle was waiting.

Behind them, in the barn, one of the cows gave a low, sleepy moo. And then another. And then the barn was quiet, except for the gentle rain, falling and falling, all through the long, soft night.

stories.title: Jam on a Wet Afternoon
stories.text:
It had been raining since breakfast. Not the loud kind of rain that rattles windows and sends people running for cover, but the steady, patient kind that settles in for the whole day, like a guest who has brought their slippers.

Sam was eight, and he had been looking forward to the park. But it was the kind of day when the park was more puddle than park, and so instead he was sitting at the kitchen table at his grandmother's house, with his chin in his hands, watching the raindrops race each other down the window.

His grandmother was called Ruth. She had silver hair tied up in a soft knot, and reading glasses on a chain around her neck, and an apron with small blue flowers on it that she had owned for longer than Sam's mother had been alive.

Well, she said, looking at the window, and then at Sam. I think this is a jam day.

A jam day? said Sam.

A jam day, said Ruth. Some days are for the park, and some days are for jam. Come and help me.

She opened the big cupboard by the back door and took out a deep, heavy pot, wide and dented and shining copper, and set it on the stove with a satisfying clunk. Then she went to the cold pantry and came back with two large bowls full of plums. They were dark purple, almost black, with a soft dusty bloom on their skins, and they had come from the old tree at the bottom of the garden.

We picked these last week, said Ruth. They've been waiting for a rainy day. Plums like the rain.

Sam was not sure that plums liked anything. But he washed his hands at the sink, and Ruth tied a spare apron around him, folded twice at the top so it would not trail on the floor, and gave him a small knife with a round tip, and showed him what to do.

You cut around the middle, like this, she said, and then you twist, gently, and the plum opens like a little book. And then you take out the stone, and put it in this bowl, and put the halves in the pot.

Sam tried. The first plum squished a little in his hand and dripped purple juice down his wrist. The second one opened perfectly, just like a little book, and he held it up so his grandmother could see.

There you go, said Ruth. You're a natural.

They worked side by side at the table. Cut, twist, stone, pot. Cut, twist, stone, pot. The rain pattered on the window. The kitchen clock ticked on the wall. Ruth's cat, a fat grey cat called Biscuit, came in from the hall, looked at the plums with deep suspicion, and went to sleep on the chair by the radiator instead.

When all the plums were in the pot, Ruth added sugar from a big paper bag, pouring it in slowly so that it made a soft, sandy hiss. Then she added a little water, and a squeeze of lemon, and lit the stove.

Now we wait, she said. And we stir. That's most of jam, really. Waiting and stirring.

She gave Sam a long wooden spoon, so old that its edge had worn flat and smooth, and a little step stool to stand on, so he could see into the pot. At first, nothing much happened. The plums sat in the pot looking purple. The sugar sat on top of them looking white. Sam stirred, slowly, round and round, and listened to the rain.

Then, little by little, the pot began to change. The sugar melted away into the juice. The plums began to soften and slump and lose their shape. A sweet, warm smell rose up from the pot, rich and deep, like autumn itself had been gathered into one place. Tiny bubbles began to appear at the edges, plip, plip, plip, and then more of them, until the whole pot was murmuring gently to itself.

It's talking, said Sam.

It is, said Ruth. That means it's happy.

While the jam cooked, Ruth washed the jars. She had a whole row of them, all different shapes and sizes, saved up over the year. Tall ones and short ones, square ones and round ones, one that had held honey and one that had held pickles and one, very small, that had once held mustard and was now Sam's favourite. She washed them in hot soapy water and set them upside down on a clean tea towel to dry, where they caught the grey light from the window and glowed.

Then she sat down at the table, and Sam stirred, and they talked about nothing in particular. About school. About Biscuit, who snored. About the time Sam's mother, when she was a little girl, had eaten a whole jar of jam with a spoon and then been too full to eat her supper.

Did she get in trouble? asked Sam.

A little, said Ruth, smiling. But mostly I laughed.

After a long while, the jam grew thick and dark and glossy, and the bubbles grew slow and heavy, plop, plop, like a very sleepy volcano. Ruth took a cold saucer from the freezer and dropped a little blob of jam onto it, and they both watched it. After a minute, she pushed it gently with her finger. The surface wrinkled.

That's how you know, she said. When it wrinkles, it's ready.

She turned off the stove. Then, very carefully, with a big ladle and a little funnel, she filled the jars one by one, while Sam held each one steady with a folded cloth. The jam poured in slow and shining, the colour of a deep red sunset, and the kitchen smelled so wonderful that even Biscuit woke up to see what was happening.

When all the jars were full, Ruth screwed on the lids, and they lined them up on the windowsill to cool. There were nine jars. Nine jars of plum jam, glowing in the soft afternoon light, with the rain falling gently behind them.

Ruth found a pen and a roll of little white labels. She wrote the first one herself, in her careful, looping handwriting. Plum jam, autumn. Then she gave the pen to Sam.

You write the rest, she said.

Sam wrote slowly, with his tongue poking out of the corner of his mouth. Plum jam. Plum jam. Plum jam by Sam and Gran. Rainy day jam. On the very smallest jar, the one that had held mustard, he wrote, for Mum, don't eat it all at once.

Ruth laughed so much she had to sit down.

Later, as the light began to fade, she cut two thick slices of bread, and toasted them, and spread them with butter, and opened the one jar that had not quite filled to the top. They sat at the table together and ate warm toast with warm jam while the rain kept falling outside, softer now, gentler, as if it too was getting sleepy.

Sam's eyes grew heavy. His grandmother's kitchen was warm, and it smelled of plums and toast, and Biscuit was purring on the chair, and the clock was ticking, and the rain was whispering on the window.

He decided that jam days might be even better than park days.

He did not say so out loud. He did not need to. His grandmother already knew.

stories.title: The Ferry Office
stories.text:
On a small island, at the very end of a stone pier, there was a little wooden hut painted the pale blue of a winter sky. Above its door hung a sign that said ferry office, and inside, behind a small counter with a brass bell on it, sat a woman called Mabel, who had worked there for most of her life.

The ferry office was not a busy place. Three times a day, the ferry came across from the mainland, chugging slowly over the grey water with its little flag flapping and its horn giving one long, low hoot as it came around the headland. Three times a day, it went back again. In between, Mabel sold a few tickets, answered a few questions, and kept the stove going, and the kettle warm, and the chalkboard up to date.

The chalkboard was the most important thing in the office. It hung on the wall beside the window, a big black board in a wooden frame, and every evening, before she went home, Mabel wrote the next day's tide times on it in neat white letters. High tide in the morning. Low tide at midday. High tide again in the evening. The islanders checked it every day on their way past, the way people in other places check the weather.

On this particular evening, it was raining. A gentle, drifting rain had come in from the sea in the late afternoon, soft and grey, and had settled over the island like a blanket. It blurred the edges of things. The lighthouse on the far point was only a pale shape in the mist. The fishing boats in the harbour rocked quietly on the water, their masts ticking against each other like slow clocks.

The last ferry of the day had already been and gone. It had brought back four people from the mainland. A fisherman with a new pair of boots. A mother and a small girl, carrying a box with holes in the lid that went peep, peep, peep. And old Mr. Pell, who went across every Thursday to buy his newspaper and a bag of peppermints and always came back looking as if he had been on a great voyage.

Now the pier was empty. The ferry was a small dark shape far away across the water, its lights growing dimmer and dimmer as it headed home for the night. Mabel watched it from the window until the mist swallowed it, and then she turned back to her little office.

She put a log on the stove. It caught with a crackle and a soft whoosh, and the warm smell of wood smoke filled the hut. She filled the kettle from the big jug and set it on top of the stove, where it began, almost at once, to tick and hum.

While she waited, she tidied the counter. She stacked the ticket books in a neat pile. She straightened the leaflets about the island's walking paths and the little museum and the seal colony on the north shore. She wound the old clock on the wall, eight slow turns of the key, and it thanked her with a deeper, steadier tick.

The rain pattered on the roof. It was a small roof, and so it made a small sound, light and quick, like a hundred tiny fingers tapping. Mabel liked it. She had always thought that rain on a small roof sounded friendlier than rain on a big one.

The kettle began to sing. Mabel made a pot of tea and poured herself a cup and sat for a moment in her chair by the stove, with her feet on the little wooden footstool her husband had made for her many years ago. She drank her tea slowly and listened to the rain and the clock and the stove, and the soft, endless whisper of the sea against the pier.

Then she got up, and took the tide book down from its shelf.

The tide book was thick and old, with a faded blue cover and pages full of tiny printed numbers. It held the times of every high tide and every low tide for the whole year. Mabel turned the pages carefully until she found tomorrow's date. She ran her finger down the column, nodding to herself.

Then she went to the chalkboard, took a cloth, and wiped away today's times. The chalk came off in soft white clouds that drifted down and settled on the floor, and the board was black and clean and waiting.

She took a fresh stick of chalk from the little box on the ledge. It was smooth and cool in her fingers. She wrote the date at the top, in her neat, round letters. Then, below it, the tides. High water, early morning, just after six. Low water, just past noon. High water again, a little before seven in the evening. She wrote slowly and carefully, the chalk making a gentle scratching sound on the board, like a mouse in the walls.

At the bottom of the board, there was a small space where Mabel wrote a note every evening. Nothing important. Just a little line for whoever happened to pass by. Sometimes it was about the weather. Sometimes it was about the seals, or the first daffodils, or the fact that the bakery on the hill had made gingerbread. People read it on their way to the ferry, and sometimes they smiled, and sometimes they wrote a little line of their own beneath it.

Tonight, Mabel thought for a while. She looked out of the window at the soft rain and the misty harbour and the boats rocking gently on the water.

Then she wrote, rain tonight, calm sea tomorrow. Sleep well, everyone.

She stepped back and looked at the board. The white letters glowed softly in the lamplight. It was good.

She washed her cup in the little sink and dried it and hung it on its hook. She let the stove burn low, and closed its door, so that it would keep a little warmth in the hut through the night. She put on her long raincoat and her woolly hat, and took her umbrella from the stand by the door.

Last of all, she turned off the lamp.

The office went dim and quiet, lit only by the faint red glow of the stove and the grey light from the window. The clock ticked. The rain pattered on the small roof. The chalkboard waited on the wall, with tomorrow's tides written on it, ready for the morning.

Mabel stepped out onto the pier and locked the door behind her. She stood for a moment under her umbrella, breathing in the cool, salty air. Out on the water, a seal lifted its head, looked at her with round dark eyes, and slipped back under without a sound.

Good night, said Mabel softly, to the seal, and to the boats, and to the sea.

Then she walked slowly back along the pier toward the village, where the windows were glowing gold in the rain, and her own small house was waiting at the top of the hill, with a warm bed and a hot water bottle and a quilt that smelled of lavender.

Behind her, the tide was turning, just as the book said it would. Gently, gently, the sea began to rise.

stories.title: The Toy Mender
stories.text:
Halfway down a cobbled street that ran gently downhill toward the river, there was a shop so small that you could walk right past it without noticing. It had a single window with a green frame and a door with a little bell, and painted on the glass, in letters that had faded to the colour of honey, were the words toys mended.

The man who mended them was called Mr. Finch. He was tall and thin, with a grey moustache and a cardigan with leather patches on the elbows, and he wore his glasses on the very end of his nose so that he could look over them at the world and through them at very small things.

His shop was full of toys waiting to be made well again. Dolls with loose arms. Wooden trains with missing wheels. A rocking horse with a torn saddle, standing patiently in the corner. A spinning top that no longer spun. Each one had a little brown tag tied to it with string, with a name written in pencil, and each one had come through the door with someone who loved it very much.

On this rainy evening, the shop was closed. The sign on the door had been turned to the side that said sorry, we're closed, come back tomorrow, and the street outside was dark and wet and shining. Rain ran in little streams between the cobbles, and dripped from the edge of the shop's green awning, plink, plink, plink, into a puddle by the step.

But inside, a lamp was still glowing on the workbench. Because there was one more toy that Mr. Finch wanted to finish tonight.

It was a bear. A small, soft, honey brown bear, with one ear slightly flatter than the other and a red ribbon tied around its neck. In its back, hidden under a little flap of fur, was a key. When you wound the key, the bear was supposed to nod its head, slowly, up and down, and play a tune. A gentle, tinkling tune, like a music box, that went round and round until it ran down and stopped.

But it had not played for a long time. The tag on its paw said, Ellie's bear. Please help. It used to play her to sleep.

Mr. Finch had been working on it since the afternoon. He laid the bear gently on its front on a folded cloth, and opened the little flap in its back, and looked inside with his small bright torch.

Inside the bear, nestled in the stuffing, was a tiny brass box. The music box. Mr. Finch lifted it out with great care, the way you might lift a sleeping bird from a nest, and set it on the bench under the lamp.

The rain drummed softly on the window. The lamp made a warm circle on the bench, and everything outside the circle was shadows and the quiet shapes of waiting toys.

Mr. Finch put on a second pair of glasses over his first pair. He picked up the smallest screwdriver he owned, so small it looked like a toy itself, and began, very slowly, to open the brass box.

There were four tiny screws. He took each one out and set it in a little saucer, where they rolled together with a sound like grains of rice. Then he lifted the lid.

Inside was a small brass drum, covered in hundreds of tiny raised pins, and beside it a little steel comb with teeth of different lengths. When the drum turned, the pins plucked the teeth of the comb, and that was what made the music. Mr. Finch had seen a great many music boxes in his life. He still thought they were one of the loveliest things anyone had ever invented.

He looked closely. And there, he saw the trouble. A tiny piece of fluff, from the bear's stuffing, had worked its way inside over the years and wrapped itself around the drum, so that it could not turn.

Ah, said Mr. Finch softly. There you are.

He took a pair of fine tweezers, and very, very gently, he began to tease the fluff away. A little at a time. A wisp here. A wisp there. He held his breath without meaning to. The clock on the wall ticked. The rain pattered. Somewhere in the corner, the rocking horse creaked very slightly, as if it were leaning in to watch.

At last, the final wisp came free. Mr. Finch set the tweezers down and let out his breath.

Then he put a single drop of oil, smaller than a tear, on the spindle where the drum turned. He wiped away every trace of dust with a soft brush. He checked the little spring, and found it tired but sound. He checked the comb, and found every tooth straight and true.

Then he closed the lid, and put back the four tiny screws, one by one, and turned the key, just once.

The drum began to turn. And out of the little brass box came a tune.

It was soft and slow and tinkling, a lullaby so old that nobody knew who had written it. It filled the little workshop like light filling a room. The notes rose up and danced around the lamp and drifted out among the waiting toys, and the rain on the window seemed to slow down to listen.

Mr. Finch sat very still until the tune ran down and stopped. Then he smiled under his grey moustache.

He nestled the music box back into the bear's stuffing, exactly where it had been. He closed the little flap, and stitched it shut with three small stitches in honey brown thread, so neat that nobody would ever find them.

And then, because he was a thorough man, he did one more thing. He took a little brush and fluffed up the bear's flat ear until it stood up properly, just like the other one. He straightened the red ribbon around its neck and tied it in a fresh bow.

Then he held the bear up under the lamp, and wound the key in its back, and set it on the bench.

The bear began to nod. Slowly, gently, up and down, up and down. And the lullaby began to play, round and round, soft and tinkling, as the rain fell softly outside on the dark, shining street.

Mr. Finch sat back in his chair and listened all the way to the end. He did not mind that it was late. He thought about a little girl called Ellie, somewhere in the town, who would come in tomorrow and pick up her bear and hold it close. He thought about her winding the key tomorrow night, in her own bed, with the rain on her window, and drifting off to sleep with the old song playing beside her pillow.

That was the best part of mending things, he thought. Not the mending itself. But knowing that tomorrow, someone would be happy.

When the last note faded, he wrote on a new tag, in careful pencil. All better. Plays beautifully. Wind gently. He tied it around the bear's paw with a little loop of string, and sat the bear on the front counter, facing the door, so it would be the first thing Ellie saw.

Then he tidied his tiny screwdrivers back into their case, and folded the cloth, and swept the last wisps of fluff into the bin. He turned off the lamp on the workbench.

The shop went dark and quiet. The rain kept falling. And on the counter by the door, the little bear sat waiting, with its key in its back and its song tucked safely inside, ready for one more night of being loved.

stories.title: The Night Train Attendant
stories.text:
The night train left the city just after nine, and by ten it was rolling through the dark countryside with a slow, steady rhythm, clickety clack, clickety clack, as if it were humming itself a song.

It was an old train, with long blue carriages and brass handles and little reading lamps in every compartment. And in the third carriage from the end, in a narrow room no bigger than a cupboard, with a small kettle and a stack of folded blankets and a neat row of tea cups on hooks, lived the attendant, whose name was June.

June had worked on the night train for many years. She knew every bend in the line and every bridge and every little station where the train slowed but never stopped. She knew which carriages ran warm and which ran cool, which windows rattled and which doors stuck. And she knew that on rainy nights like this one, people slept better than on any other night of the year.

The rain had begun as the train left the city. Now it was falling steadily, streaming down the windows in long silver lines that wobbled and joined and ran sideways in the wind. Through the glass, the world outside was dark and soft and blurry. Now and then a single light went by, a farmhouse window or a lamp at a crossing, glowing gold for a moment and then gone.

June put on her navy jacket with the brass buttons, and pinned her little name badge to the front, and picked up her clipboard. It was time to make up the berths.

She started at the front of the carriage. The first compartment held an elderly couple who were going to visit their grandchildren by the sea. They were sitting side by side by the window, holding hands, watching the rain.

Good evening, said June. Shall I make up your beds?

Oh, yes please, said the woman. We were just saying how cosy it is, with the rain.

It's the best kind of night for the train, said June, and she meant it.

She folded the seats down into beds. She shook out the crisp white sheets and tucked them in with sharp, neat corners, the way she had been taught a long time ago. She plumped the pillows until they were round and soft. She laid a thick wool blanket over each bed, dark blue with a thin gold stripe, and turned down the top corner, just a little, so that the bed looked as if it were saying, come in.

Would you like a cup of tea before you settle? she asked.

They would. Everyone always would.

June went back to her little room and filled the kettle and set it on its tiny stove. While it warmed, she leaned against the doorway and listened to the train. Clickety clack, clickety clack. The soft creak of the carriages as they leaned around a bend. The rain on the roof, a steady, gentle drumming that you felt more than heard.

When the kettle sang, she made two cups of tea and set them on a little tray with two shortbread biscuits, and carried them down the swaying corridor without spilling a single drop. That was a skill that had taken her years to learn. Now she could do it with her eyes closed.

The next compartment held a young man with a guitar case, who was travelling home for the first time in a long while. He had fallen asleep sitting up, with his head against the window and his coat over his knees. June did not wake him. She took a blanket from her arm and laid it gently over him, and turned his reading lamp down low, and slid the door closed without a sound.

The compartment after that held a mother and a little boy in striped pyjamas, who was much too excited to sleep. He was kneeling on the seat with his nose pressed to the window, trying to see the rain in the dark.

Where are we? he asked June.

Somewhere very quiet, said June. In the middle of the night, in the middle of the country, in the middle of the rain.

He thought about this. It seemed to satisfy him.

June made up the beds, the top bunk for the boy, the bottom for his mother. She showed him the little ladder, and the little reading lamp, and the little net pocket on the wall where he could keep his book. Then she reached into her jacket pocket and gave him something she kept there for exactly this kind of occasion. It was a small paper ticket, old fashioned, with a hole punched in one corner and the words night train printed across it.

Your ticket to sleep, she said. Keep it under your pillow.

The boy took it very seriously. He climbed up the ladder, tucked the ticket under his pillow, and lay down. By the time June had brought his mother a cup of cocoa, his eyes were already closing.

Down the carriage she went, compartment by compartment. A woman knitting a long red scarf, who wanted only a glass of water. Two sisters sharing a bag of toffees, who wanted extra pillows. A man in a grey suit with a briefcase full of papers, who looked very tired, and who smiled when June brought him a cup of tea he had not asked for, and closed his briefcase, and did not open it again.

By midnight, every bed was made, and every lamp was low, and every door was closed. The corridor was quiet and dim, lit only by small night lights near the floor that glowed a soft amber, like embers. June walked slowly along it one last time, listening.

She heard the soft breathing of people asleep. A cough. A sigh. A page turning. Somewhere, very quietly, the young man with the guitar was humming in his sleep.

And under it all, the train. Clickety clack. Clickety clack. And the rain, drumming gently on the roof, mile after mile after mile.

June went back to her little room. She hung up her jacket. She made herself one last cup of tea and sat on her small fold down seat by the window, with a blanket of her own over her knees.

Outside, the dark country rolled by. The rain streamed down the glass. Far away, on a hill, a single light was burning in a farmhouse window, and June wondered who was awake there, and whether they could hear the train going by, a long line of glowing windows in the rain, carrying all these sleeping people through the night.

She hoped they could. She thought it must be a comforting sound, from far away.

The train leaned gently into a long bend. The cups swayed on their hooks with a tiny clink. June finished her tea, and rested her head against the cool window, and closed her eyes for just a moment.

Clickety clack. Clickety clack.

The rain fell, and the train rolled on, and everyone aboard was sleeping, safe and warm, all the way to morning.

outro:
And that is the end of tonight's stories.

The lock gates are closed on the quiet canal. The bread is cooling on Elm Lane, and the cat has passed every loaf. A grey coat hangs ready for the cold. Eleven cows are warm in the barn. Nine jars of plum jam are glowing on a windowsill. Tomorrow's tides are written on the chalkboard, a little bear is waiting by the door with its song inside, and the night train is still rolling on through the rain.

There are more quiet stories waiting on the channel, whenever you need them.

Good night, and sleep well.
thumb_subtitle: 8 gentle stories on a rainy night
description:
Eight cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly with soft rain in the background to help you unwind and drift off.
A lock keeper on a quiet canal, a baker's cat, a tailor's last coat, cows coming home, plum jam with Gran, an island ferry office, a toy mender's music box bear and a night train attendant.
No drama, no cliffhangers, just calm.
Good night 🌙
